question: A lathe is a machine tool used mainly to produce which kind of objects?
explanation: The lathe is employed generally to produce cylindrical objects by rotating the work against a single-point tool.

question: Which machine tool is often called the "mother of all machine tools"?
explanation: The handout calls the lathe the mother of all machine tools, because most other machine tools developed from it.

question: Turning on a lathe removes excess material from the work to produce which kind of surface?
explanation: Turning produces cylindrical or tapered (cone-shaped) surfaces on rotating work.

question: Which of these is NOT one of the types of lathe listed in the ME-106 lathe handout?
explanation: The handout lists engine, speed, turret, capstan and CNC lathes. "Slotting" is a different machine (a vertical shaper), not a lathe type.

question: The most commonly used general-purpose lathe in engineering workshops is the…
explanation: The engine lathe (centre lathe) is the general-purpose lathe found in most workshops, including our machine shop.

question: What is the working principle of a lathe?
options: Both tool and work reciprocate in straight lines
The work rotates while a single-point tool is fed against it
The tool rotates while the work is fed against it
An abrasive wheel rotates against fixed work
explanation: On a lathe the workpiece rotates and a single-point cutting tool is given feed motion. In milling and grinding it is the cutter or wheel that rotates.
ref: Centre Lathe handout p.2; Manufacturing notes p.11–12

question: In which of these machines does the WORKPIECE rotate while the tool is fed?
explanation: In a lathe the work rotates; in milling and grinding the cutter or wheel rotates, and in a shaper the tool reciprocates.

question: For metal cutting on a lathe there must always be relative motion between the tool and the workpiece.
explanation: Cutting needs relative motion: the work rotates and the tool is fed, as noted in the lathe notes.

question: Centre-lathe turning belongs to which group of manufacturing processes?
explanation: Turning removes metal as chips, so it is a metal-removal (machining) process.

question: Which group of parts is mounted on the CARRIAGE of a centre lathe?
options: Tailstock quill, dead centre and handwheel
Lead screw, feed rod and legs
Saddle, cross-slide, compound rest and tool post
explanation: The carriage slides on the bed and carries the saddle, cross-slide, compound rest and tool post (with the apron hanging in front).
ref: Centre Lathe lecture slide 7; Centre Lathe handout p.4

question: Which part of a lathe is the main supporting structure on which the headstock, tailstock and carriage are mounted?
explanation: The bed is the principal supporting structure; the headstock, tailstock and carriage are all mounted on it.

question: On a lathe, the tailstock and carriage slide along the…
options: Guideways (bedways) on top of the bed
Threads of the lead screw under the bed
Keyway cut along the length of the feed rod
Dovetail slide on top of the cross-slide
explanation: The tailstock and carriage move over the guideways machined on the top face of the bed.

question: Lathe beds are generally made of which material?
explanation: The lecture states lathe beds are generally grey cast iron because of its damping, rigidity and self-lubricating qualities.

question: Why is grey cast iron used for lathe beds?
options: Good damping, rigidity and self-lubricating quality
Low density and high electrical conductivity
High red hardness at cutting temperatures
explanation: Grey cast iron damps vibration well, is rigid, and its graphite gives a self-lubricating surface on the ways.

question: According to the lathe handout, a good lathe bed material should have which two properties?
options: Low hardness and high electrical conductivity
High compressive strength and high wear resistance
High ductility and high thermal expansion
explanation: The handout says bed material needs high compressive strength and high wear resistance; nickel-chromium alloyed cast iron is a good choice.

question: Lathe bed guideways are of two types. Which pair is correct?
explanation: The lecture names the two types of guideways as inner ways and outer ways.

question: On which side of the lathe bed is the headstock mounted (operator facing the lathe)?
explanation: The headstock is on the left-hand side of the bed; the tailstock is on the right.
ref: Centre Lathe handout p.3; Centre Lathe handout p.4

question: Which lathe part houses the main spindle, the speed-change gear box and the change gears?
explanation: The headstock houses the main spindle, speed-change mechanism and change gears.

question: Besides varying spindle speed, the headstock gear box also…
options: Transmits power to the feed rod and lead screw
Moves the tailstock along the bed guideways
Locks the carriage in place for parting-off
Holds the dead centre in line with the spindle
explanation: The headstock gear box varies spindle speed and transmits power to the feed rod and lead screw.

question: The chuck or face plate of a lathe is attached to the…
explanation: The chuck or face plate is mounted on the headstock spindle, which grips and rotates the work.

question: Which part of the lathe carries the LIVE centre?
explanation: The live centre sits in the headstock spindle and rotates with the work. The tailstock carries the dead centre.

question: Which part of the lathe carries the DEAD centre?
explanation: The tailstock carries the dead centre, which does not rotate; the headstock spindle carries the live centre.

question: Which of these is a function of the tailstock?
options: Giving the different speed changes to the spindle
Engaging the half-nut on the lead screw for threading
Swivelling the tool post to the angle for tapers
Supporting long work and holding drills or reamers
explanation: The tailstock supports the free end of the work and holds tools such as drills, reamers and taps.

question: Why can the tailstock be moved along the bed?
options: To change the speed of the main spindle
To accommodate workpieces of different lengths
To set the pitch of the thread being cut
To lock the carriage in position for facing
explanation: The tailstock slides on the guideways so work of different lengths can be supported.

question: Which of these is a part of the TAILSTOCK?
explanation: The tailstock has a body, adjustable base, spindle (quill), feed screw handwheel and a locking lever.

question: Which part of the lathe supports, moves and controls the cutting tool?
explanation: The carriage serves as the supporting, moving and controlling part of the cutting tool.

question: The H-shaped part of the carriage that fits over the bed and slides along the ways is the…
explanation: The saddle is H-shaped, fits over the bed, slides along the guideways and can be locked in any position.

question: Movement of the saddle parallel to the lathe axis gives the…
explanation: Saddle movement along the axis is the (longitudinal) feed; cross-slide movement sets the depth of cut.

question: Which part moves the lathe tool at right angles to the lathe axis?
explanation: The cross-slide sits on the saddle and moves the tool perpendicular to the work axis.

question: On a lathe, the depth of cut is set by moving the…
explanation: The perpendicular distance moved by the cross-slide (via its handwheel) is the depth of cut.

question: The compound rest is mounted directly on top of the…
explanation: The compound rest (top slide) is mounted on the cross-slide, and the tool post sits on the compound rest.

question: Which lathe part has a base graduated in degrees and is used for short tapers and angular cuts?
explanation: The compound rest swivels on a base graduated in degrees for angular cuts and tapers.

question: In taper turning by the compound-rest method, how is the feed given?
options: By hand, with the compound-slide handwheel
Automatically, through the lead screw and half-nut
Automatically, through the feed rod and apron
By setting the tailstock over from the axis
explanation: The compound slide has no power feed; its handwheel is turned by hand to feed the tool along the taper.
ref: Centre Lathe lecture slide 19; Centre Lathe lecture slide 21

question: Which part holds the cutting tool rigidly on a lathe?
explanation: The tool post is mounted on the compound rest and clamps the tool rigidly.

question: Which of these is NOT a type of lathe tool post?
explanation: The lecture lists single-screw, four-way and eight-way tool posts.

question: The carriage handwheel, half-nut lever and feed lever are located on the…
explanation: The apron hangs in front of the carriage and contains the carriage handwheel, half-nut lever and feed lever.

question: Which shaft drives the carriage or cross-slide for turning, boring and facing (not threading)?
explanation: The feed rod transmits power from the feed box to move the carriage or cross-slide for ordinary feeds.

question: The lead screw of a lathe is used for…
explanation: The lead screw is a long threaded shaft used only for thread cutting; it is disengaged for normal turning.

question: For thread cutting, the carriage is connected to the lead screw through the…
explanation: Closing the half-nuts on the lead screw makes the carriage advance exactly one pitch per spindle revolution.

question: Which part of a lathe collects the chips and coolant that fall from the work?
explanation: The chip tray (chip pan) under the bed collects chips; the legs support the machine.

question: On the lathe headstock, the tumbler gears are used to…
options: Lock the spindle for chuck changing
explanation: The lecture lists tumbler gears for forward/reverse and engage/disengage of the feed drive.

question: Which of the three lathe feeds is given ONLY by hand?
explanation: Longitudinal and cross feeds can be by hand or power; angular feed (compound slide swivelled) is hand-operated only.

question: Feed given by swivelling the compound slide to the required angle is called…
explanation: There are three feeds: longitudinal (parallel to axis), cross (perpendicular) and angular (compound slide swivelled).

question: Which of these is NOT used to specify a centre lathe?
options: Number of teeth on the chuck jaws
explanation: A lathe is specified by bed length, distance between centres, swing over bed and carriage, power, lead-screw pitch, speeds, feeds and bed width.

question: The "swing" of a lathe means…
options: The angle through which the compound rest swivels
The largest work diameter that can rotate over the bed
The distance moved by the carriage per revolution
explanation: Swing is the largest diameter of work that can be swung (rotated) over the lathe bed.

question: Which of these is NOT a standard way of holding work on a lathe?
explanation: Work is held between centres, on a mandrel, in a chuck, on a face plate/angle plate or in a collet. Magnetic chucks with dogs are a grinding-machine feature.

question: When work is turned between centres, what actually drives (rotates) the workpiece?
options: Friction between the work and the dead centre
The lead screw acting through the half-nut
The tailstock quill pressing on the work end
A lathe dog clamped to the work, driven by the catch plate
explanation: A dog (carrier) is clamped to the work and its tail is driven by the catch (dog) plate on the spindle.

question: In which chuck do all the jaws move together, so the work is centred automatically?
explanation: In a 3-jaw (self-centring) chuck all three jaws move simultaneously; in a 4-jaw chuck each jaw moves independently.

question: A 3-jaw self-centring chuck is suitable for holding which work?
explanation: The 3-jaw chuck holds cylindrical and hexagonal work; irregular shapes need a 4-jaw chuck.

question: In a 4-jaw chuck the jaws…
options: All move together through a scroll
Move independently, each by its own screw
explanation: Each jaw of a 4-jaw (independent) chuck is moved separately, so the work must be centred manually.

question: Which chuck is preferred for holding an irregular or square workpiece?
explanation: The independent jaws of a 4-jaw chuck can grip irregular shapes, which a self-centring chuck cannot.

question: What is the main drawback of a 4-jaw independent chuck compared with a 3-jaw chuck?
options: It grips the work far less firmly than a 3-jaw
It cannot be used for facing the end of the job
The work must be centred manually, which takes time
It cannot hold round work of any diameter
explanation: Because the jaws move independently, the work has to be trued (centred) by hand; a 3-jaw chuck centres automatically.
ref: Centre Lathe lecture slide 24; Theory: Hajra Choudhury

question: Which statement about 4-jaw chuck jaws is correct?
options: They are fixed and cannot be adjusted
explanation: The lecture states the jaws of a 4-jaw chuck are reversible and each moves independently.

question: Compared with a 3-jaw chuck, a 4-jaw independent chuck…
options: Cannot be used with HSS tools
Grips less firmly but centres automatically
Grips more firmly but is slower to set up
explanation: A 4-jaw chuck gives a stronger grip and holds any shape, but centring is manual. A 3-jaw chuck is quick to set because it self-centres.

question: A collet holds bar stock by…
options: Being squeezed onto the bar through its slits
Magnetic attraction between collet and bar
Four independent jaws, each worked by a screw
Friction between the bar and the dead centre
explanation: A collet has slits (three in the lecture) so a sleeve can squeeze it onto the bar.

question: Irregular work that cannot be held in a chuck is clamped to the…
explanation: A face plate is attached to the spindle and work is bolted/clamped to it.

question: Chuck jaws are tightened and loosened using a…
explanation: A chuck key turns the chuck screw (or scroll) to move the jaws; always remove it before starting.

question: In the ME-106 lathe lab, which items were used for MARKING the job?
options: Vernier height gauge and angle plate
Chalk, marker, marking stand and marking plate
Scriber, dot punch and centre punch
explanation: The ME-106 lathe log sheet lists chalk, marking stand, marking plate and marker as the marking tools.

question: In the ME-106 lathe lab, the diameter of the job was checked with an…
options: Dial indicator on a magnetic stand
explanation: The log sheet lists an outside caliper and scale for measuring the job.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.1; Theory: Hajra Choudhury

question: Which of these is NOT in the list of tools used in the ME-106 lathe lab?
explanation: The lathe log sheet lists chalk, marking stand, marking plate, outside caliper, scale, marker, lathe job carrier and catch. A dividing head is a milling accessory.

question: In the ME-106 lathe lab, the job was held in which device?
explanation: The procedure says to fix the workpiece in the four-jaw chuck after marking 115 mm.

question: The 2025 ME-106 lathe log sheet adds which items to the tool list?
explanation: The 2025 log sheet also lists a lathe tool holder, a wrench and the chuck.

question: An outside caliper has no scale. How is the measured diameter read?
options: By transferring the setting to a steel rule
Directly from the Vernier scale on its legs
From a dial gauge fixed on its hinge
From the cross-slide dial of the lathe
explanation: An outside caliper only transfers a size; you read it by placing the legs against a steel rule.

question: What is the workpiece material of the ME-106 lathe job?
explanation: The lathe notes state the job is low-carbon steel, i.e. mild steel.

question: Mild (low-carbon) steel contains approximately…
explanation: Mild steel is low-carbon steel with less than about 0.3% C. 0.6–1.5% is high-carbon steel and 2–4% C is cast iron.

question: The cutting tool used on the lathe in the ME-106 lab is made of…
explanation: The lathe notes and log sheets use an HSS single-point tool.

question: Which basic rule applies to the tool and workpiece materials in machining?
options: The tool must be harder than the workpiece
Hardness does not matter in turning
The workpiece must be harder than the tool
explanation: The tool must always be harder than the material it cuts.

question: The common 18-4-1 high-speed steel contains about…
explanation: 18-4-1 HSS has 18% tungsten, 4% chromium and 1% vanadium (with ~0.7% C).

question: Why is high-speed steel called "high speed" steel?
options: It is made by a high-speed rolling process
It cools down quickly after cutting
It can only be used at high spindle speeds
It keeps its hardness at high cutting temperatures
explanation: HSS retains its hardness (red hardness) at the high temperatures produced by high-speed machining.

question: Medium-carbon steel contains about…
explanation: Standard ranges: low < 0.3%, medium 0.3–0.6%, high 0.6–1.5% C. (The class notebook says 1.5–2% for medium-carbon steel. That is wrong; see corrections.md #1.)

question: An iron–carbon alloy with about 3% carbon is classed as…
explanation: Steel contains up to about 2.1% C. Above that the alloy is cast iron. 6.67% C corresponds to cementite (Fe₃C).

question: High-carbon steel contains about…
explanation: High-carbon steel has roughly 0.6–1.5% C. 6.67% C is cementite, not a steel.

question: Which of these is NOT a part of a single-point cutting tool?
explanation: Single-point tool parts are shank, face, flank, heel, base, nose and point. Tang is part of a file.

question: On a single-point tool, the surface over which the chip flows is the…
explanation: The face is the top surface over which the chip slides; the flank faces the work below the cutting edge.

question: The angle that prevents the tool flank from rubbing against the work is the…
explanation: The clearance (relief) angle gives the flank room so it does not rub on the machined surface.

question: Which tool angle mainly helps the chip flow away and reduces the cutting force?
explanation: Rake angle is the slope of the tool face; a positive rake eases chip flow and lowers cutting force.

question: Which lathe operation produces a flat surface at the end of the work and reduces its length?
explanation: Facing machines the end of the work flat; the tool is fed perpendicular to the axis.

question: In facing, the tool is fed…
explanation: In facing the tool moves across the face, perpendicular to the axis (cross feed).

question: Which operation reduces the diameter of the work along its whole length?
explanation: Straight turning reduces the diameter along the length; the tool is fed parallel to the axis.

question: Reducing the diameter over only part of the length, leaving shoulders of different diameters, is called…
explanation: Step turning gives steps (shoulders) of different diameters along the job.

question: The operation of bevelling the sharp end edge of a turned job is…
explanation: Chamfering creates a slope at the end edge to remove burrs and sharp corners; our job has a 1 × 45° chamfer.

question: Knurling on a lathe is done to…
options: Cut a helical thread on the surface
Emboss a pattern on the surface for grip
Cut off the finished job from the bar
Enlarge an already drilled hole to size
explanation: A knurling tool is pressed against the rotating work to emboss a diamond or straight pattern, e.g. on handles.

question: A narrow recess cut at the end of a thread (as in our job) is made by…
explanation: Grooving uses a tool shaped to the groove; the ME-106 job has a 5 mm groove next to the thread.

question: In parting-off on a lathe…
options: The carriage is locked and the tool is plunged radially
The tool is fed parallel to the lathe axis
The compound rest is swivelled to 45° and fed
The lead screw drives the tool along the work
explanation: Parting cuts the job off the bar; longitudinal feed is fixed and the tool is fed in radially until the work separates.

question: Why is a centre hole drilled at the end of the workpiece?
options: To hold the knurling tool during knurling
To start the thread at the correct pitch
To reduce the weight of the finished job
So the work can be supported between centres
explanation: Centre drilling makes a conical seat so the work can be held on a centre (between centres) in any machine.

question: Which tool is used for centre drilling on a lathe?
options: Centre drill held in the tailstock
Parting tool in the tool post
explanation: A combined centre drill is held in a drill chuck in the tailstock and fed into the rotating work.
ref: Manufacturing notes p.14; Centre Lathe handout p.4

question: A uniform decrease in diameter along the length of the work is called a…
explanation: A taper is a uniform change of diameter along the length, specified by the difference in diameters over the length.

question: Which of these is NOT a method of taper turning on a lathe?
explanation: Taper-turning methods: compound rest, form tool, tailstock set-over and taper-turning attachment. Straddle is a milling set-up.

question: Which taper-turning method suits a long, gentle taper on work held between centres?
explanation: Setting the tailstock over suits long, gentle tapers between centres. The compound rest suits short, steep tapers.

question: The compound-rest method of taper turning is best suited for…
explanation: The compound slide has limited travel, so it is used for short tapers with large angles.

question: Which taper-turning method needs a tool whose cutting edge is ground to the taper angle?
explanation: In the form-tool method a broad tool with an edge at the taper angle is plunged in; it suits very short tapers.
ref: Centre Lathe lecture slide 10, s.19; Theory: Hajra Choudhury

question: Boring on a lathe…
explanation: Boring enlarges an already-drilled hole; reaming finishes a hole to size.

question: In form turning, the shape produced on the work is obtained by…
options: Setting over the tailstock from the axis
Swivelling the compound rest to an angle
A tool ground to the required profile
Engaging the lead screw and half-nut
explanation: Form turning reproduces the tool profile on the work, e.g. convex or concave forms.

question: Which of these operations is NOT normally done on a centre lathe?
explanation: Lathe operations include facing, turning, taper turning, threading, knurling, drilling, boring, reaming and parting. Gear hobbing needs a hobbing machine.

question: Why is the centre lathe called a versatile machine?
options: It cuts on both the forward and return strokes
One machine can face, turn, thread, drill, bore and knurl
It works without any cutting tool at all
It cuts gears using an index plate and crank
explanation: A single centre lathe performs many operations: facing, turning, taper turning, threading, drilling, boring, knurling and parting.

question: For which kind of part is a centre lathe LEAST suitable?
explanation: The lathe suits rotationally symmetric parts. Flat slotted plates are milled or shaped. Lathes are also slow for mass production compared with capstan/turret/CNC.

question: Thread cutting on a lathe produces a…
options: Helical groove on a cylindrical surface
Straight groove parallel to the axis
explanation: A screw thread is a helical groove; any pitch, shape and size can be cut on a lathe with a single-point tool.

question: During thread cutting, how far must the tool advance per revolution of the work?
explanation: The lead screw drives the carriage so that the longitudinal feed per revolution equals the pitch.

question: The distance between corresponding points on adjacent threads, measured along the axis, is the…
explanation: Pitch is the axial distance between adjacent threads; crest is the top, root the bottom and flanks the sides.

question: The included angle of a metric (ISO) V-thread is…
explanation: Metric threads have a 60° included angle. 55° is the Whitworth angle and 29° is the Acme angle.

question: In the thread designation M20 × 1.5, what do 20 and 1.5 stand for?
explanation: "M" means metric; 20 mm is the major (nominal) diameter and 1.5 mm the pitch.

question: The formula used in our lab for the depth of a metric thread is…
explanation: The lab log sheets and notes use d = 0.6134 p for the thread depth (depth of cut).

question: The core (minor) diameter of a thread is given by…
explanation: The core diameter equals the major diameter minus twice the thread depth: Dc = Dm − 2d.

question: Square threads are mainly used in…
explanation: Square threads transmit power with low friction, so they are used in load-lifting devices like screw jacks.

question: A buttress thread is used where…
options: Fluid-tight joints in pipes are needed
Only light fastening of thin parts is needed
Heavy load must be transmitted in one direction only
Equal load must be carried in both directions
explanation: A buttress thread has one steep flank and one inclined flank; it carries heavy one-way loads, e.g. in vices.

question: In the ME-106 lathe lab, why was the spindle speed reduced to about 90 rpm for threading?
options: The lead screw cannot be rotated above 90 rpm
HSS tools soften and melt above 90 rpm
Slow speed gives time to withdraw the tool at the groove
Facing has to be repeated at the lower speed
explanation: Turning was done at 315 rpm but threading at about 90 rpm. In threading the carriage moves fast (one pitch per revolution), so a low speed gives time to withdraw the tool at the end of each pass.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.2; Log Sheets ME-106 p.1

question: Cutting speed in turning is calculated as…
explanation: Cutting speed V = πDN/1000 m/min, with D in mm and N in rpm (surface speed of the work).

question: In the ME-106 lathe job, a Ø38 mm bar is turned at 315 rpm. What is the cutting speed?
explanation: V = πDN/1000 = π × 38 × 315 / 1000 ≈ 37.6 m/min. Forgetting π gives 12.0; mis-dividing gives 376 or 3.76.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Log Sheets ME-106 p.1

question: The Ø34 thread of the ME-106 job is cut at 90 rpm. What is the cutting speed?
explanation: V = π × 34 × 90 / 1000 ≈ 9.61 m/min. Leaving out π gives 3.06 m/min.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Log Sheets ME-106 p.2

question: In turning, "feed" means…
options: Thickness of metal removed in one pass
Surface speed of the work in m/min
Number of passes needed to finish the job
Distance the tool advances per revolution of the work
explanation: Feed is measured in mm/rev. Depth of cut is the radial thickness removed in a pass.

question: A bar is turned from Ø38 mm to Ø34 mm in one pass. What is the depth of cut?
explanation: Depth of cut = (D − d)/2 = (38 − 34)/2 = 2 mm. 4 mm is the reduction in diameter, not the depth of cut.

question: What was the least count of the cross-slide dial on the ME-106 lathe?
explanation: The lathe log sheet notes the cross-slide least count as 0.02 mm.

question: Each division of the cross-slide dial moves the tool 0.02 mm radially. The dial is advanced by 25 divisions for one cut. By how much does the work DIAMETER reduce?
explanation: 25 × 0.02 = 0.5 mm radial depth of cut. Metal comes off all round, so the diameter reduces by 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 mm.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.1; Theory: Hajra Choudhury

question: To reduce a diameter from 38 mm to 34 mm with a depth of cut of 0.5 mm per pass, how many passes are needed?
explanation: Radial material = (38 − 34)/2 = 2 mm; 2 / 0.5 = 4 passes. Using the full diameter difference gives 8.

question: In the formula tan α = (D − d)/2L for taper turning, α is…
options: The helix angle of the thread
The rake angle of the tool
The full included angle of the cone
explanation: α is the half taper angle, which is the angle the compound rest is swivelled to.

question: For the ME-106 lathe job, the taper goes from Ø38 to Ø34 over 30 mm. What is tan α?
explanation: tan α = (38 − 34)/(2 × 30) = 4/60 = 1/15. Forgetting the 2 gives 2/15.
ref: Centre Lathe handout p.12; Central Lathe Log sheet p.1

question: At what angle should the compound rest be set to turn the taper on the ME-106 job (Ø38 → Ø34 over 30 mm)?
explanation: α = tan⁻¹[(38 − 34)/(2 × 30)] = tan⁻¹(0.0667) ≈ 3.81°. Forgetting the 2 gives 7.59°; the full cone angle is 2α ≈ 7.63°.
ref: Centre Lathe handout p.12; Central Lathe Log sheet p.2

question: A taper is turned from Ø50 mm to Ø40 mm over a length of 100 mm. What is the half taper angle?
explanation: tan α = (50 − 40)/(2 × 100) = 0.05, so α ≈ 2.86°. Forgetting the 2 gives tan α = 0.1, i.e. 5.71°.

question: On the ME-106 taper (Ø38 → Ø34), how much material is removed from the RADIUS at the small end?
explanation: Radial reduction = (38 − 34)/2 = 2 mm at the small end; the diameter reduces by 4 mm.
ref: Central Lathe Log sheet p.1; Theory: Hajra Choudhury

question: For the ME-106 job taper (Ø38 → Ø34 over 30 mm), the taper ratio (D − d) : L is…
explanation: (D − d) : L = 4 : 30 = 1 : 7.5. The 1 : 15 figure is tan α, i.e. half of this ratio.
ref: Centre Lathe handout p.12; Central Lathe Log sheet p.1

question: Using d = 0.6134 p, what is the thread depth for the 1.5 mm pitch thread on the ME-106 job?
explanation: d = 0.6134 × 1.5 = 0.920 mm. 1.84 mm is 2d; 0.61 mm is the factor without the pitch.
ref: Manufacturing notes p.15; Central Lathe Log sheet p.2

question: What is the core diameter of the Ø34 × 1.5 thread on the ME-106 lathe job?
explanation: Dc = Dm − 2d = 34 − 2(0.92) = 32.16 mm. Subtracting d once gives 33.08 mm; adding gives 35.84 mm.
ref: Manufacturing notes p.15; Central Lathe Log sheet p.2

question: For an M20 × 2.5 thread, what is the core diameter (using d = 0.6134 p)?
What is the thread depth for a 2 mm pitch metric thread (d = 0.6134 p)?
On a lathe, a thread of 1.5 mm pitch is being cut. How far does the carriage move in 20 revolutions of the work?
explanation: During threading the tool advances one pitch per revolution: 20 × 1.5 = 30 mm.

question: What is the objective of the ME-106 lathe job?
options: To cut a spur gear on an aluminium disc
To finish a flat steel surface by grinding
To perform facing, turning and threading on a cylindrical workpiece
To reduce a block to 38 × 21 × 73 mm on a shaper
explanation: The lathe log sheet objective: perform facing, turning and threading operations on a cylindrical workpiece using a lathe.

question: According to the ME-106 lathe notes, what was the raw stock size?
options: Mild-steel bar about 120 mm long, Ø38 mm
explanation: The lathe notes give the workpiece as 120 mm long and 38 mm in diameter.

question: A 120 mm bar (as recorded in the lathe notes) is faced to the 115 mm overall length. How much length is removed by facing in total?
explanation: Raw length 120 mm − finished 115 mm = 5 mm removed in total by facing (shared between the two ends).
ref: Manufacturing notes p.17; Central Lathe Log sheet p.1

question: What is the overall length of the finished ME-106 lathe job?
explanation: The job drawing shows an overall length of 115 mm (raw bar 120 mm).

question: Units used on the ME-106 lathe job drawing are…
explanation: The board drawing states "All dimensions are in mm". (The milling gear job uses inches.)

question: What is the correct order of the first four steps of the ME-106 lathe job?
options: Mark 115 mm and fix in 4-jaw chuck → facing → measure the bar → set speed
Set speed → facing → mark 115 mm and fix in 4-jaw chuck → measure the bar
Measure the bar → mark 115 mm and fix in 4-jaw chuck → centre and set speed → facing
Facing → measure the bar → mark 115 mm and fix in 4-jaw chuck → set speed
explanation: Log sheet steps 1–4: measure length and diameter; mark 115 mm and fix in the four-jaw chuck; check centre and set 315 rpm; perform facing.

question: What is the FIRST step of the ME-106 lathe procedure?
options: Measure the length and diameter of the raw workpiece
Set the spindle to 90 rpm for threading
Swivel the compound rest to the taper angle
Perform facing to bring the job to length
explanation: Step 1 is to measure the length and diameter of the raw workpiece; then mark and fix it in the chuck.

question: In the ME-106 lathe procedure, which step comes immediately AFTER fixing the job in the four-jaw chuck?
options: Check the centring and set the spindle speed
Taper turning with the compound rest
Removing the job to measure it again
explanation: After chucking, the centre is checked (4-jaw work is centred manually) and the speed set to 315 rpm, then facing is done.

question: In the ME-106 lathe lab, the spindle speed set for facing and turning was about…
explanation: The log sheet and notes record 315 rpm for turning; threading was done at about 90 rpm.

question: Why must the job be checked for centring after fixing it in the four-jaw chuck?
options: The tailstock moves automatically during cutting
The lead screw has to be aligned with the job
The thread pitch has to be set from the centre
Its jaws move independently, so the job is not self-centred
explanation: A 4-jaw chuck does not self-centre, so the job is trued manually before cutting.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.1; Centre Lathe lecture slide 24

question: In the ME-106 lathe job, facing is done to…
options: Bring the job to the desired length
Turn the taper at the end
explanation: Step 4: perform facing on the workpiece to get the desired length (115 mm).

question: In the 2025 ME-106 lathe log sheet, which step comes immediately after facing?
options: Grooving and taper turning in the marked areas
explanation: The 2025 sheet: measure → mark & chuck → centre & set rotation → facing → groove and taper turn → threading.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.1; Central Lathe Log sheet p.1

question: In the ME-106 lathe procedure, which of these is done first?
explanation: Facing to length comes before grooving, taper turning and threading.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.1; Central Lathe Log sheet p.1

question: Which step comes immediately BEFORE thread cutting in the ME-106 lathe procedure?
options: Fixing the job in the chuck
explanation: The log sheet sequence ends: … groove (5 mm) and taper turning with the compound rest → threading at reduced speed.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.2; Central Lathe Log sheet p.1

question: How is the taper on the ME-106 job turned?
options: By swivelling the compound rest to the half-taper angle
By setting the tailstock over from the axis
With a broad form tool plunged straight in
By engaging the lead screw and half-nut
explanation: The log sheet sets the tool post/compound rest at the calculated angle and turns the taper.

question: Before cutting the 1.5 mm pitch thread on the ME-106 job, the operator…
options: Swivels the compound rest to 3.81° for the taper
Engages the feed rod for power cross feed
Removes the four-jaw chuck and fits a collet
Sets the change gears from the chart and reduces speed
explanation: The log sheet says to look at the table (chart) for 1.5 mm pitch, arrange the gears and set the speed to about 90 rpm.

question: Which is the correct sequence of steps on the 2025 ME-106 lathe log sheet?
options: Mark 115 mm & fix in 4-jaw chuck → threading → facing → measure → centre & set rotation → groove & taper turning
Measure → threading → facing → groove & taper turning → mark 115 mm & fix in 4-jaw chuck → centre & set rotation
Facing → measure → threading → mark 115 mm & fix in 4-jaw chuck → groove & taper turning → centre & set rotation
Measure → mark 115 mm & fix in 4-jaw chuck → centre & set rotation → facing → groove & taper turning → threading
explanation: The 2025 log sheet lists these six steps in this order.
ref: Central Lathe Log sheet p.1; Log Sheets ME-106 p.1

question: Besides facing, turning, taper turning, grooving and threading, which other operations appear on the ME-106 lathe job drawing?
explanation: The drawing shows centre holes at both ends and a 1 × 45° chamfer.

question: Which dress precaution is given on the ME-106 lathe log sheet?
options: Wear loose, comfortable clothes and sandals
Wear the workshop apron, tight-fitting clothes and shoes
Roll up sleeves loosely and wear a tie
Wear gloves while the chuck is rotating
explanation: The log sheet precaution: always wear the manufacturing apron, tight-fitted clothes and shoes.

question: According to the ME-106 lathe log sheet, chips should be…
options: Removed in time, to avoid accidents
Left until the job is finished
Pulled off by hand while cutting
explanation: Remove chips timely to avoid accidents — and use a brush or chip hook, never bare hands.

question: Why does the 2025 lathe log sheet ask students to stay at a proper distance from the machine?
options: Hot chips may fly off the work
The lead screw is live electrically
The tailstock moves on its own
explanation: Chips at high temperature can fly off, so stand at a proper distance.

question: Which precaution about measuring is given on the 2025 lathe log sheet?
options: Measure only while the job rotates
Measure in proper lighting with inside and outside calipers
Measure only after removing the job from the chuck
Measure with the chuck key left in place
explanation: Take good measurements in proper lighting using inner and outer calipers.

question: Before switching on the lathe, you must always…
options: Engage the half-nut on the lead screw
Loosen the tool post clamping screw
Remove the chuck key from the chuck
Remove the tailstock from the bed
explanation: A chuck key left in the chuck is thrown out violently when the spindle starts.

question: When should the lathe job be measured with a caliper?
options: While the chuck is rotating slowly
explanation: Always stop the lathe before measuring the job or changing speeds/gears.

question: Which of these is a precaution specific to the ME-106 lathe log sheet?
options: Demagnetise the chuck before removing the job
Do not rotate the index crank backwards
Do not touch the plating solution
explanation: The lathe log sheet lists: apron/tight clothes/shoes, handle heavy machines with care, remove chips timely, move the tailstock carefully.

question: Which precaution appears on both ME-106 lathe log sheets?
options: Never switch the coolant pump off
Dress the wheel before every cut
Handle heavy machines and tools with care
explanation: Both lathe sheets say to handle heavy machines and tools with care.

question: Which of these is UNSAFE practice on the lathe?
options: Removing chips with bare hands while the lathe runs
Removing the chuck key before starting
Using a brush to clear chips after stopping
explanation: Chips are sharp and hot. Clear them with a brush or hook after stopping the machine.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.1; Theory: Hajra Choudhury

question:
Assertion (A): A 3-jaw chuck cannot hold a rectangular block securely.
Reason (R): The jaws of a 3-jaw chuck move together and centre round or hexagonal work.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: Both are true and R explains A: because the three jaws move together on a scroll, they suit only round or hexagonal shapes, so irregular work needs a 4-jaw chuck.

question:
Assertion (A): The lead screw is disengaged during ordinary plain turning.
Reason (R): The lead screw is used only for thread cutting.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: Both are true and R explains A: the lead screw is reserved for threading (to keep it accurate); the feed rod gives ordinary feeds.

question:
Assertion (A): HSS is used for the lathe tool in the ME-106 lab.
Reason (R): HSS is softer than mild steel, so it does not chip.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: A is true but R is false: HSS is much harder than mild steel. The tool must be harder than the work, and HSS keeps its hardness at cutting temperatures.
ref: Manufacturing notes p.11, p.17; Manufacturing notes p.11

question:
Assertion (A): Threading on the ME-106 lathe was done at a lower spindle speed than turning.
Reason (R): The lead screw is used only for thread cutting.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: Both are true, but R does not explain A. The low speed is used because the carriage advances one pitch per revolution, which is fast at turning speeds, so the operator could not withdraw the tool in time at the groove.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.2; Centre Lathe handout p.7

question: The tailstock of a lathe carries the live centre.
explanation: False. The headstock spindle carries the live centre, which rotates with the work. The tailstock carries the dead centre, which does not rotate.
ref: Centre Lathe lecture slide 14; Centre Lathe lecture slide 15

question: In turning, the depth of cut equals half the reduction in diameter.
explanation: True. Depth of cut = (D − d)/2, because metal is removed all round the work.

question: In the ME-106 (2025) job, the threaded portion is 25 mm long.
explanation: True. The Ø34 × 1.5 thread runs for 25 mm, between the 5 mm groove and the Ø32 end section.

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Headstock. Houses the main spindle, speed gear box and change gears; carries the live centre.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Chuck. Grips and rotates the workpiece; attached to the headstock spindle.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Bed. Main supporting structure on which headstock, tailstock and carriage are mounted.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
explanation: D = Tailstock. Supports the free end of long work; holds drills and reamers.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = Dead centre. Non-rotating centre in the tailstock that supports the work.
label: E

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled F?
explanation: F = Tailstock quill (spindle). Sliding spindle of the tailstock that carries the dead centre or a drill.
label: F

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled G?
explanation: G = Tailstock handwheel. Moves the tailstock quill in and out.
label: G

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled H?
explanation: H = Saddle. H-shaped part of the carriage that slides along the bed ways.
label: H

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled I?
explanation: I = Cross-slide. Moves the tool at right angles to the lathe axis; sets depth of cut.
label: I

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled J?
explanation: J = Compound rest. Swivelling top slide used for short tapers and angular cuts.
label: J

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled K?
explanation: K = Tool post. Holds the cutting tool rigidly on top of the compound rest.
label: K

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled L?
explanation: L = Apron. Front of the carriage; contains the carriage handwheel, half-nut and feed levers.
label: L

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled M?
explanation: M = Lead screw. Long threaded shaft used only for thread cutting.
label: M

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled N?
explanation: N = Feed rod. Plain shaft that drives the carriage for turning and facing feeds.
label: N

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled O?
explanation: O = Leg. Supports the whole machine on the floor.
label: O

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled P?
explanation: P = Gear box (feed box). Gives different feeds and thread pitches; drives the feed rod and lead screw.
label: P

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled Q?
explanation: Q = Chip tray. Collects chips and coolant falling from the work.
label: Q

question: In the figure, which label shows the tailstock?
explanation: D = Tailstock. Supports the free end of long work; holds drills and reamers.
label: D

question: In the figure, which label shows the saddle?
explanation: H = Saddle. H-shaped part of the carriage that slides along the bed ways.
label: H

question: In the figure, which label shows the compound rest?
explanation: J = Compound rest. Swivelling top slide used for short tapers and angular cuts.
label: J

question: In the figure, which label shows the lead screw?
explanation: M = Lead screw. Long threaded shaft used only for thread cutting.
label: M

question: In the figure, which label shows the feed rod?
explanation: N = Feed rod. Plain shaft that drives the carriage for turning and facing feeds.
label: N

question: In the figure, which label shows the apron?
explanation: L = Apron. Front of the carriage; contains the carriage handwheel, half-nut and feed levers.
label: L

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled A?
options: Houses the main spindle, speed gear box and change gears; carries the live centre
Plain shaft that drives the carriage for turning and facing feeds
Collects chips and coolant falling from the work
Grips and rotates the workpiece; attached to the headstock spindle
explanation: A = Headstock. Houses the main spindle, speed gear box and change gears; carries the live centre.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled I?
options: Non-rotating centre in the tailstock that supports the work
Moves the tool at right angles to the lathe axis; sets depth of cut
Gives different feeds and thread pitches; drives the feed rod and lead screw
Sliding spindle of the tailstock that carries the dead centre or a drill
explanation: I = Cross-slide. Moves the tool at right angles to the lathe axis; sets depth of cut.
label: I

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled K?
options: Moves the tailstock quill in and out
Long threaded shaft used only for thread cutting
Front of the carriage; contains the carriage handwheel, half-nut and feed levers
Holds the cutting tool rigidly on top of the compound rest
explanation: K = Tool post. Holds the cutting tool rigidly on top of the compound rest.
label: K

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled P?
options: Gives different feeds and thread pitches; drives the feed rod and lead screw
Collects chips and coolant falling from the work
Front of the carriage; contains the carriage handwheel, half-nut and feed levers
Moves the tailstock quill in and out
explanation: P = Gear box (feed box). Gives different feeds and thread pitches; drives the feed rod and lead screw.
label: P

question: Which chuck is shown in panel A?
explanation: A = 3-jaw (self-centring) chuck. All three jaws move together through a scroll, so round or hexagonal work is centred automatically.
label: A

question: Which chuck is shown in panel B?
explanation: B = 4-jaw (independent) chuck. Each jaw has its own screw and moves independently, so irregular work can be held but must be centred manually.
label: B

question: In the figure, which chuck must have the work centred manually?
explanation: Panel B is the 4-jaw independent chuck. Each jaw is moved separately, so the job is centred by hand, as was done in our lab.

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Catch (driving) plate. Screwed on the spindle nose; its pin drives the tail of the dog.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Live centre. Centre in the headstock spindle that rotates with the work.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Lathe dog (carrier). Clamped to the work by a set screw and driven by the catch plate.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
explanation: D = Workpiece. Job held and turned between the two centres.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = Dead centre. Non-rotating centre in the tailstock that supports the free end.
label: E

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled F?
explanation: F = Tailstock quill. Tailstock spindle that carries the dead centre.
label: F

question: Which lathe operation is shown in panel A?
explanation: A = Facing. Flat end surface; tool fed perpendicular to the axis; reduces length.
label: A

question: Which lathe operation is shown in panel B?
explanation: B = Straight (plain) turning. Diameter reduced along the length; tool fed parallel to the axis.
label: B

question: Which lathe operation is shown in panel C?
explanation: C = Step turning. Diameter reduced over part of the length, leaving a shoulder.
label: C

question: Which lathe operation is shown in panel D?
explanation: D = Taper turning. Uniform change of diameter along the length; tool fed at the half-taper angle.
label: D

question: Which lathe operation is shown in panel E?
explanation: E = Grooving. Narrow groove cut by plunging a grooving tool radially.
label: E

question: Which lathe operation is shown in panel F?
explanation: F = Parting-off. Tool plunged radially until the finished job is cut off.
label: F

question: Which lathe operation is shown in panel G?
explanation: G = Chamfering. Bevels the sharp end edge (e.g. 45°) to remove burrs.
label: G

question: Which lathe operation is shown in panel H?
explanation: H = Centre drilling. Conical centre hole drilled from the tailstock so the work can be supported on a centre.
label: H

question: Which lathe operation is shown in panel I?
explanation: I = Thread cutting. Helical groove cut by a single-point tool fed one pitch per revolution.
label: I

question: Which lathe operation is shown in panel J?
explanation: J = Knurling. Pattern pressed (embossed) on the surface by knurling rollers.
label: J

question: Which panel shows taper turning?
explanation: D = Taper turning. Uniform change of diameter along the length; tool fed at the half-taper angle.
label: D

question: Which panel shows parting-off?
explanation: F = Parting-off. Tool plunged radially until the finished job is cut off.
label: F

question: Which panel shows centre drilling?
explanation: H = Centre drilling. Conical centre hole drilled from the tailstock so the work can be supported on a centre.
label: H

question: Which panel shows thread cutting?
explanation: I = Thread cutting. Helical groove cut by a single-point tool fed one pitch per revolution.
label: I

question: Which thread profile is shown in panel A?
explanation: A = Metric V-thread. Fastening threads (bolts, nuts, screws); 60° included angle.
label: A

question: Which thread profile is shown in panel B?
explanation: B = Square thread. Power/load transmission such as screw jacks and lead screws.
label: B

question: Which thread profile is shown in panel C?
explanation: C = Buttress thread. Transmits heavy load in one direction only, e.g. vices.
label: C

question: What is the thread form in panel A typically used for?
options: Pipe joints that must be fluid-tight
Fastening threads (bolts, nuts, screws); 60° included angle
Rounded threads for rough use, e.g. railway couplings
Transmits heavy load in one direction only, e.g. vices
explanation: A = Metric V-thread. Fastening threads (bolts, nuts, screws); 60° included angle.
label: A

question: What is the thread form in panel B typically used for?
options: Fastening threads (bolts, nuts, screws); 60° included angle
Pipe joints that must be fluid-tight
Power/load transmission such as screw jacks and lead screws
Transmits heavy load in one direction only, e.g. vices
explanation: B = Square thread. Power/load transmission such as screw jacks and lead screws.
label: B

question: What is the thread form in panel C typically used for?
options: Transmits heavy load in one direction only, e.g. vices
Rounded threads for rough use, e.g. railway couplings
Pipe joints that must be fluid-tight
Fastening threads (bolts, nuts, screws); 60° included angle
explanation: C = Buttress thread. Transmits heavy load in one direction only, e.g. vices.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Crest. Top surface of the thread.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Root. Bottom of the groove between two threads.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Flank. Side surface joining crest and root.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
explanation: D = Pitch. Axial distance between corresponding points on adjacent threads.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = Depth of thread. Radial distance between crest and root (d = 0.6134 p for our metric thread).
label: E

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled F?
explanation: F = Major diameter (radius shown). Largest diameter of the thread, measured over the crests.
label: F

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled G?
explanation: G = Minor (core) diameter (radius shown). Smallest diameter, at the roots: Dc = Dm − 2d.
label: G

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Shank. Main body of the tool held in the tool post.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Nose. Corner where the side and end cutting edges meet.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Face. Top surface over which the chip flows.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
explanation: D = Flank. Surface below the cutting edge, facing the work.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = Base. Bottom surface of the shank that rests on the tool post.
label: E

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled F?
explanation: F = Rake angle. Slope of the face; eases chip flow and lowers cutting force.
label: F

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled G?
explanation: G = Clearance (relief) angle. Angle of the flank that stops it rubbing on the work.
label: G

question: In the ME-106 lathe job drawing, what is the diameter of section P?
explanation: Section P is the Ø38 plain section, 35 mm long, with a 1 × 45° chamfer at the left end.
label: P

question: In the job drawing, what is the length of the taper Q?
explanation: The taper runs from Ø38 to Ø34 over 30 mm.
label: Q

question: In the job drawing, what is the width of the groove R?
explanation: A 5 mm groove separates the taper from the thread.
label: R

question: What is the thread specification of section S on the job drawing?
explanation: Section S is threaded Ø34 × 1.5 mm pitch, 25 mm long.
label: S

question: What are the diameter and length of the end section T on the job drawing?
explanation: Section T at the right end is Ø32 mm and 20 mm long.
label: T

question: What chamfer is specified at the left end of the ME-106 lathe job?
explanation: The drawing calls for a 1 × 45° chamfer at the left end of the Ø38 section.
ref: Central Lathe Log sheet p.1; Centre Lathe handout p.10

question: From the job drawing, how far from the LEFT end does the threaded portion start?
explanation: Left end → Ø38 (35) → taper (30) → groove (5): 35 + 30 + 5 = 70 mm. The thread then runs to 95 mm.

question: The job drawing shows small conical marks at both ends on the axis. They indicate…
explanation: Both ends of the ME-106 job are centre-drilled so the work can be supported on centres.
ref: Central Lathe Log sheet p.1; Manufacturing notes p.14

question: From the job drawing, what is the sum of the lengths of the taper and the thread?
explanation: Taper 30 mm + thread 25 mm = 55 mm.

question: In the ME-106 lathe job, at what stage is the length of 115 mm marked on the bar?
options: After the thread has been cut
After the taper has been turned
After parting the job off the bar
Before fixing the bar in the four-jaw chuck
explanation: Step 2 of the log sheet: mark 115 mm on the workpiece and fix it in the four-jaw chuck.

question: Which lathe part is swivelled during the taper-turning step of the ME-106 job?
explanation: For taper turning the compound rest (tool post slide) is set at the half-taper angle (≈3.81°) and fed by hand.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.2; Centre Lathe lecture slide 19

question: During the threading step of the ME-106 job, what drives the carriage along the work?
options: Feed rod via the apron gears
explanation: For threading the half-nut is engaged on the lead screw so the carriage moves exactly one pitch (1.5 mm) per revolution.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.2; Centre Lathe handout p.7

question: In the ME-106 job, the 5 mm groove is cut…
options: Before the job is faced to length
Before the raw bar is measured
After the thread has been finished
After facing, together with taper turning, before threading
explanation: The log sheet cuts the 5 mm groove after step turning, then turns the taper and finally cuts the thread up to the groove.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.2; Central Lathe Log sheet p.1

question: Where is the tool tip set when a lathe tool is clamped in the tool post?
options: Exactly at centre height (level with the lathe axis)
Well above the axis to increase clearance
Well below the axis to avoid rubbing
explanation: The tip must be on the lathe axis. Above or below centre changes the effective rake and clearance and leaves a pip when facing.

question: After facing, a small pip is left at the centre of the job face. What is the likely cause?
options: The tool tip is not at centre height
The spindle speed is too high
explanation: A pip at the centre is the classic sign that the tool is above or below centre height.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Centre Lathe handout p.9

question: Why should the tool overhang from the tool post be kept short?
options: To make the taper angle steeper
To engage the lead screw more easily
To keep the tool rigid and avoid chatter
To increase the cutting speed of the work
explanation: A long overhang makes the tool spring and vibrate (chatter); keep it short and clamp firmly.

question: How is a job centred in a four-jaw chuck?
options: Rotate by hand, check run-out with chalk/surface gauge and adjust opposite jaws
Bring up the tailstock and press the job hard
Run the lathe at high speed and watch the chips form
Tighten all four jaws together with one key turn
explanation: With independent jaws, the job is trued by turning the chuck by hand and adjusting opposite jaws in pairs until run-out is removed.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Log Sheets ME-106 p.1

question: Which order of cuts gives the best finish and size control on a lathe?
options: Finishing cut first, then rough cuts
Rough cuts first, then a light finishing cut
Alternate deep and light cuts at random
explanation: Rough cuts remove most of the metal quickly; a final light cut with fine feed gives finish and accurate size.

question: For a final finishing cut on the lathe you would use…
options: Large depth of cut and coarse feed
Large depth of cut and fine feed
Small depth of cut and fine feed
explanation: Finishing cuts are light (small depth) with fine feed for good surface finish.

question: Which is the correct order for cutting a thread on a centre lathe?
options: Engage half-nut → set gear box for pitch → set tool square with centre gauge → take one deep cut
Set gear box for pitch → set tool square with centre gauge → engage half-nut → take light successive cuts
Take light successive cuts → set gear box for pitch → engage half-nut → set tool square with centre gauge
Set tool square with centre gauge → take light successive cuts → set gear box for pitch → engage half-nut
explanation: Set the pitch first, square the 60° tool with a centre gauge, engage the half-nut and take several light cuts, withdrawing the tool after each pass.

question: Which gauge is used to set a threading tool square to the work and check its 60° angle?
explanation: A centre gauge has 60° notches; it is used to grind the thread tool and set it square to the work.

question: How is the finished thread on the lathe job checked?
options: With a try square held against the flanks
With a screw-pitch gauge or a mating nut
With an outside caliper and steel rule only
By comparing its colour with the bar
explanation: Pitch is checked with a screw-pitch gauge; fit is checked by running a mating nut on.

question: At the end of each threading pass, the operator should…
options: Withdraw the tool, then return the carriage for the next cut
Leave the tool in the groove and reverse at full depth
explanation: The tool is withdrawn with the cross-slide at the end of each pass, the carriage is returned, and the next light cut is taken.

question: Before switching on the lathe after setting up a job, you should…
options: Switch on at the highest speed to test
Turn the chuck once by hand to check clearances
explanation: Rotating the chuck by hand confirms that the jaws and job clear the tool and carriage.

question: In the ME-106 lathe procedure, which spindle speeds were used for (i) turning and (ii) threading?
explanation: Turning was done at about 315 rpm and threading at a reduced speed of about 90 rpm.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.1; Log Sheets ME-106 p.2

question: In the ME-106 job, which operation finishes the job last according to the procedure?
explanation: The final step listed on the log sheets is to perform threading over the marked 25 mm length.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.2; Central Lathe Log sheet p.1

question: What should you do if your hand gets close to the rotating chuck?
options: Never touch it; never try to stop the chuck by hand
Grab the job firmly to stop it
Use a cloth to brake the chuck gently
Slow the chuck down with your palm
explanation: Never touch the rotating job or chuck, and never stop it by hand. Switch off and let it come to rest.

question: When is it safe to change the spindle speed or gears on the lathe?
options: Only when the machine is stopped
explanation: Gears and speed levers are changed only after the spindle has stopped.

question: Before drilling with a drill held in the tailstock, you must…
options: Lock the tailstock to the bed
explanation: An unlocked tailstock is pushed back by the drilling thrust; lock the tailstock (and quill) first.

question: Which eye protection should be worn on the lathe?
explanation: Flying chips can injure the eyes, so wear safety goggles.

question: Which of these is a safe practice on the lathe?
options: Leaving the chuck key in the chuck between jobs
Keeping the bed ways clear of tools while cutting
Leaning on the carriage while it is cutting
Wearing a loose tie and open sleeves
explanation: Do not keep tools on the bed or carriage, do not lean on the machine, and remove the chuck key.

question: Why must the tool and job be clamped firmly before starting the lathe?
options: To increase the cutting speed of the job
To reduce the pitch of the thread cut
To keep the tool cool during cutting
A loose tool or job can be thrown out or dig in
explanation: Firm clamping prevents the job or tool from loosening, digging in or flying out.

question: Which of these is NOT a lathe-shop precaution?
options: Remove the chuck key before starting
Stop the chuck by hand to save time
explanation: Stopping the chuck by hand is dangerous. The others are standard precautions on the lathe log sheets and in workshop practice.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Log Sheets ME-106 p.1

question: A student leaves the chuck key in the chuck and switches on. What is the danger?
options: The pitch of the thread changes suddenly
The lead screw disengages from the half-nut
The key is thrown out with great force
The tailstock locks itself to the bed
explanation: The spinning chuck flings the key out, which can seriously injure people nearby. Always remove the key first.

question: Tight-fitting clothes are required in the lathe shop because…
options: Loose clothing can be caught by the rotating chuck or work
They help in marking the job with chalk
They keep the coolant off the operator
They protect the operator from electric shock
explanation: Loose sleeves, ties or clothes can be pulled into rotating parts.

question: The correct way to clear long chips from a lathe is to…
options: Ignore them until the job ends
Stop the machine and use a brush or chip hook
Blow them away with your mouth
Pull them away by hand while cutting
explanation: Chips are sharp and hot. Remove them in time with a brush or hook, never with bare hands.

question: It is acceptable to measure the lathe job with a caliper while it is rotating slowly.
explanation: False. Always stop the machine before measuring.

question: Why does the lathe log sheet ask you to move the tailstock carefully?
options: It carries the live centre that drives the job
It controls the speed of the main spindle
It is heavy and can hit the carriage or run off the bed
It holds the lead screw used for threading
explanation: The tailstock is a heavy casting; sliding it roughly can damage the ways, hit the carriage or run off the end of the bed.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.1; Centre Lathe handout p.4

question: Why should measurements on the lathe be taken in proper lighting?
options: So caliper settings are read accurately
So that the chips cool down faster
So that the motor runs cooler
So that the thread pitch does not change
explanation: Calipers have no scale; a correct reading against the rule needs good light, as stated on the 2025 log sheet.
ref: Central Lathe Log sheet p.1; Theory: Hajra Choudhury

question: A long, continuous chip is winding around the rotating job. What should you do?
options: Pull it off quickly by hand before it tangles
Cut it with pliers while the lathe keeps running
Increase the spindle speed so the chip breaks
Stop the lathe, then remove the chip with a hook or brush
explanation: Never handle chips on a running machine. Stop it, then use a chip hook or brush.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.1; Theory: Hajra Choudhury

question: Which item of PPE is NOT normally required for the ME-106 lathe practice?
explanation: Lathe work needs an apron, tight clothes, shoes and eye protection; laser goggles are for the fiber laser.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.1; Theory: Hajra Choudhury

question: Which precaution protects the operator from HOT chips specifically?
options: Stand at a proper distance and wear goggles
Set the tool at centre height
Use the lead screw only for threading
explanation: Hot chips can fly, so keep a proper distance (2025 log sheet) and protect your eyes.
ref: Central Lathe Log sheet p.1; Theory: Hajra Choudhury

question: Before starting the lathe, which check prevents the chuck jaws from hitting the carriage?
options: Rotate the chuck once by hand
explanation: Hand-rotating the chuck shows whether the jaws or job foul the tool or carriage.

question: In the ME-106 lathe job, which marking tools are used in the marking step?
options: Chalk, marker, marking stand and plate
Surface gauge, angle plate and scriber
explanation: The job is marked using chalk/marker with the marking stand and marking plate, then measured with scale and outside caliper.

question: Which measuring tools are used in step 1 of the ME-106 lathe procedure?
explanation: The raw length and diameter are measured with the steel scale and outside caliper.

question: Why is threading done LAST in the ME-106 lathe job?
options: Threading has to be done before facing the ends
The thread must run up to the groove, which is cut earlier
The lead screw can be used only after facing
Threading removes the 1 × 45° chamfer at the end
explanation: The thread is cut last, up to the 5 mm groove that was cut earlier; turning after threading would damage the thread.
ref: Central Lathe Log sheet p.1; Log Sheets ME-106 p.2

question: What is engaged for plain turning but NOT used for threading?
explanation: Ordinary turning feed comes from the feed rod; threading uses the lead screw and half-nut.
ref: Centre Lathe handout p.7; Central Lathe Log sheet p.1
